uncited: It builds on [Plenoxels Optimization Configuration](929-plenoxels-optimization-configuration.md) by adding depth constraints to the optimization process.
- RGB-D image pair (color $C$, depth $D$) from a camera pose $P$.
- Pre-existing Plenoxel radiance field model (voxel grid with opacity $\sigma$ and spherical harmonic coefficients).
- Updated Plenoxel model parameters (refined geometry and appearance).
- Refined camera pose $P'$ (in the context of tracking).
- Voxel grid storing radiance field parameters.

- Outward-facing scenes: Standard NeRF fails to capture geometry; depth sensors ensure accurate geometry [S1].

The claim states that Standard NeRF fails to capture geometry in outward-facing scenes and that depth sensors ensure accurate geometry. The evidence explicitly supports this: Source [S1] notes state, 'Unlike NeRF which suffers from geometric ambiguity in outward-facing scenes, this method uses depth sensors to ensure accurate geometry.' Additionally, the passages mention that scenes with sparse gradient coverage (characteristic of outward-facing scenes) are 'incapable of capturing the geometry' and that using RGB-D sensors 'removes ambiguities in gradient-less regions'.

The optimization minimizes the photometric difference between the observed image and the image rendered from the estimated pose [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the authors 'implement a pose optimization algorithm to track a camera throughout the scene, using volumetric, dense image-to-model alignment based on the radiance field rendering equations.' Image-to-model alignment in this context inherently involves minimizing the difference (photometric error) between the observed image and the rendered image from the estimated pose to achieve accurate tracking and mapping.
